posts.title: Preject Page Building. Assissted by Figma MCP & Cursor.
posts.content:
It has been verified that Cursor can use Figma MCP to build web pages for the designs I created. Note that users must have a Figma membership, including the education version or the full version. Generated code and verified page blow（package needs typograpy file)

Preparations
Meet the Basic Requirements
Have a Figma account (education version or full version is acceptable).
Install the latest version of the Cursor editor.
Install Node.js (version 18.0 or above). After installation, open the terminal and run the node -v command to verify the successful installation.
Prepare a package manager such as npm, pnpm, yarn, or bun.
Obtain the Figma API Token
This token is used for authenticating the connection between Cursor and Figma.
Log in to your Figma account (either on the web or desktop version).
Click your avatar in the upper right corner and select "Settings".
Find "Personal access tokens" in the left menu, click "Create new token", enter a name (like "Cursor MCP"), and then click "Create token".
Immediately copy the generated token starting with figd_ and keep it properly, as it will be used for subsequent configurations.

Core Configuration Steps
a. Configure the Figma MCP Server in Cursor
             This step establishes a communication bridge between Cursor and Figma. The NPX method is recommended for easier operation:
Open the Cursor editor. Press Ctrl + Shift + P (for Windows) or Cmd + Shift + P (for Mac) to open the command panel.
Search for "MCP" or "Model Context Protocol" and select the configuration option to open the MCP configuration file.
Add the following configuration code. Remember to replace "your API token" with the Figma token you copied earlier.

b. Set the Access Permission of the Figma Design File
             This step establishes a communication bridge between Cursor and Figma. The NPX method is recommended for easier operation:
Open the design file you created in the desktop version of Figma.
Click the "Share" button in the upper right corner and set the permission to "Anyone with the link can view" to ensure iii. Cursor can read the file.
Cursor can read the file.

Generate Web Pages from Designs
Initiate the Conversion Command in Cursor
Open the chat panel in Cursor. You can press Ctrl + L (for Windows) or Cmd + L (for Mac), or directly click the chat icon.
Paste the copied Figma file link, and then send a clear instruction to generate a web page. For example: "Please convert this Figma design into a responsive HTML and CSS web page" or "Turn this design into a React component web page".
If you want to operate a specific element in the design, right-click the element in Figma, copy its link, paste it into Cursor, and add instructions targeting that element (such as "Generate the code of this button and integrate it into the homepage").
Optimize and Verify the Generated Code
After Cursor generates the code, you can check the code structure, styles, and layout in the editor. Modify parameters such as colors and spacing according to needs.
Create a new file (like index.html) in Cursor, paste the generated code, and then use a browser to open the file to preview the web page effect.
If there are issues like inconsistent styles with the design, you can send supplementary instructions to Cursor (e.g., "Adjust the button spacing to be consistent with the Figma design") for code optimization.

posts.title: Zero Cost: Building My Pixel-Art Blog with React
posts.content:
If you want a personalized, lightning-fast, and completely free digital space without the headache of managing servers and databases, this "backend-less" pixel-art blog architecture is the perfect blueprint.

 The Tech Stack: The Art of Frontend
Built with React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, the project focuses on a "retro-gaming" aesthetic. I used localized pixel fonts to ensure a consistent look with a loading time of under 50ms.

Design Style: 8-bit retro vibes featuring a sleek black background paired with vibrant pink and purple accents.

Deployment: Hosted on GitHub Pages (100% free).

Resource Management: External image hosting and embedded video links keep the repository lightweight.

The Core Innovation: Backend-less Persistence
The most unique feature of this project is how it handles data without a traditional database. How can everyone see my posts without a backend?

I designed a "Local Edit + Git Storage" loop:

Publishing: After a password check on the frontend, data is saved to the browser’s localStorage.

Export: A built-in tool allows one-click export of posts into a JSON file.

Global Sync: By placing the exported JSON into the project's public/data/ folder and pushing it to GitHub, the content becomes part of the source code.

Smart Loading:

The app prioritizes localStorage for an instant "cold start."

If the cache is empty, it fetches the JSON data from GitHub, ensuring the content is synced for all visitors.

✨ Key Features
Content Management: Full CRUD logic (Create, Read, Update, Delete) built directly into the UI.

Multimedia Support: Seamless display for multiple images and embedded video players.

Offline-First: All fonts and styles are localized, maintaining high performance even on slower networks.

💡 Why This Approach?
For indie developers, "getting it running" is often more important than "perfection." This architecture offers three ultimate advantages:

Zero Cost: No server fees, no database subscriptions.

Minimal Maintenance: Updating your blog is as simple as a Git commit. Your Git history acts as a natural backup.

Extreme Performance: As a purely static site, the initial load time is typically under 2 seconds.

posts.title: CAD Design Practice. (Gear Dragonfly & Sword)
posts.content:
Design process video demonstration below：Gear. Racks. Housing. Grips.


* GB/T 1804-m
According to GB/T 1804-m grade tolerance, the letter "m" represents the medium precision grade (medium tolerance class). It applies to uncharted linear dimensions, rounded radii, and chamfer heights on general engineering drawings. This grade provides economical machining accuracy achievable under normal workshop processing conditions and is typically used for non-fit dimensions. For example, if the tolerance allowed by the functional requirement of a dimension is larger than the general tolerance, the tolerance may be omitted from the drawing and inspection is generally not required. A case in point: the limit deviation for dimensions greater than 30 mm up to 120 mm is ±0.3 mm.
Meaning of Tolerance Grade (m Grade) in GB/T 1804
Grade SelectionGB/T 1804 specifies four tolerance grades: f (fine), m (medium), c (coarse), and v (very coarse). Among these, 'm' denotes medium precision, which is equivalent to ISO 2768-1-m (the international standard).
Scope of ApplicationIt is primarily used for dimensions without directly marked tolerances after dimensioning (uncharted tolerance dimensions), such as linear dimensions, angular dimensions, rounded radii, and chamfer heights.
EconomyIt reflects the economical accuracy attainable with standard workshop processes and equipment, and is suitable for fitting parts with low precision requirements.
Examples of GB/T 1804-m Grade
Baidu Experience (see text for data source) provides the limit deviation values for linear dimensions under GB 1804-M:
0 ~ 3 mm: ±0.1 mm
3 ~ 6 mm: ±0.1 mm
6 ~ 30 mm: ±0.2 mm
30 ~ 120 mm: ±0.3 mm


专业术语注释（确保技术准确性）
未注公差尺寸 → uncharted tolerance dimensions（工程领域规范译法，区别于 "untoleranced dimensions"）
经济加工精度 → economical machining accuracy（强调工艺成本与精度的平衡）
非配合尺寸 → non-fit dimensions（对应机械设计中 “无装配精度要求的尺寸”）
极限偏差 → limit deviation（公差领域核心术语，不可译作 "limit error"）
格式说明
保留标准编号 GB/T 1804-m 和 ISO 2768-1-m 的原始格式（国际标准编号通用惯例）
公差等级 f/m/c/v 采用括号加注中文释义的形式，便于双语对照
尺寸区间和偏差值的表示完全遵循工程英文书写规范（如 ±0.3 mm 无空格）

posts.title: Arduino Input/Output and Laser Cutting：Rococo Lumina
posts.content:
Interactive Digital Firework Installation: Rococo Lumina

Project Overview
This project is an art installation that combines Arduino physical interaction with Processing visual programming. Users interact with the device via an HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor, which controls the perspective and intensity of the digital fireworks on the screen:

- Closer Distance: The fireworks appear larger and more spectacular, emphasizing an immersive experience.
- Farther Distance: A wider perspective is revealed, showcasing a panoramic view of the fireworks filling the sky.
The core highlights of this project are its unique visual style and the AI-Assisted Development (AICD) process employed during the design phase.

✨ Visual Style Evolution: From Manga Rays to Rococo Halos
The visual style was the focal point of the project's iteration, achieved through a series of advanced customizations guided by the AI:

- Initial Goal: Based on the reference image , the initial style was set to multi-colored, high-contrast digital fireworks, emphasizing sharp lines and geometric structure (similar to Manga/Anime aesthetics).
First Iteration (Style Solidification): By optimizing particle rendering logic, the introduction of dual-layer lines and high-light tips achieved the desired high-contrast, radially symmetric explosion effect.
- Second Iteration (Dreamlike Transition): Adopting user feedback for a more ethereal visual, the style shifted. By incorporating blendMode(ADD), slower particle speeds, and using gradually dissipating particle dots instead of hard line segments, the visual successfully transitioned from sharp "rays" to soft "halos" and "particle trails."
- Final Style (Rococo Customization): The final aesthetic was locked into the Rococo art style. The AI created a fixed, refined color palette consisting of rose pink, sky blue, creamy yellow, etc., and optimized transparency control within the HSB color mode. This resolved the critical issue of colors being drowned out by the white overlay in the additive blend mode, achieving an elegant, soft, yet vividly colored artistic effect.

posts.title: Practical Guide: 8051 Microcontroller LED Chaser PCB Design
posts.content:
Phase 1: Scheme Selection & Requirement Iteration (Project Kickoff)
At the start of the project, we underwent a strategic shift from a complex architecture to a more beginner-friendly one:

Initial Scheme: We originally planned to use an ESP32. However, considering the soldering difficulty for a beginner (dense pins and complex peripheral circuitry), we pivoted to the classic STC89C516.

Package Selection: To balance size and ease of assembly, we avoided ultra-small components and chose the LQFP-44 package for the MCU (reasonable pin pitch) paired with 0603 surface-mount resistors and LEDs.

Download Logic: For ultimate simplification, we removed the onboard USB-to-Serial chip (CH340). Instead, we reserved a 4-pin header to allow programming via an external USB-to-TTL module.

Phase 2: Schematic Logic Correction (Core Problem-Solving)
During the schematic design, multiple real-time AI reviews helped identify and bridge several "critical pits":

Power Recognition (USB-C Specific): We added 5.1kΩ pull-down resistors on the CC1/CC2 pins. This ensures that modern E-marker cables (C-to-C) correctly recognize the board and provide 5V power.

EA Pin (8051 Specific): We hard-wired Pin 31 (EA) to VCC. Without this, the MCU would attempt to read from external memory, causing it to "freeze" upon startup.

Reset Circuit Correction: We redesigned the reset logic from a shorted state to a proper High-Level Reset structure. This uses a 10µF capacitor to VCC and a 10kΩ resistor to GND, with the midpoint connected to Pin 4 (RST).

Current-Limiting Adjustment: We corrected the LED resistors from 10kΩ (which would make the LEDs too dim to see) to 1kΩ, ensuring vibrant illumination.

Phase 3: PCB Layout & Routing
Transitioning to the PCB phase, we followed the "Signal Integrity First" principle:

Crystal Placement: The 11.0592MHz crystal and its two 30pF capacitors were placed as close as possible to Pins 14 and 15 to minimize clock signal interference.

Interface Placement: The USB-C port was placed at the board's edge for easy access.

Routing Self-Check: We utilized "ratsnest" (airwire) prompts to systematically connect the power grid (VCC/GND) and signal traces.

Copper Pouring: After routing, we performed a GND Copper Pour (Ground Plane) across the entire board to reduce noise and simplify ground connections.

Phase 4: The Last Line of Defense Before Ordering
In the final review, we caught several critical routing omissions:

Missing Traces: Although airwires existed, the RST and XTAL pins had not been physically routed with copper traces. These were manually connected before finalizing.

DRC Check: We used the software's built-in Design Rule Check (DRC) to eliminate "Floating Pin" warnings and ensure no shorts existed.


* Design Takeaways for Fellow Readers
1. Verify Pin Definitions: Never trust the default pin names in a library blindly. Pins like EA are mission-critical for the chip to function.
2. Schematic First, PCB Second: If the logic isn't connected correctly in the schematic, the PCB will never work.
3. Soldering Friendliness: For your first board, use "Long Pad" versions of footprints. While 0603 is the comfort limit for hand-soldering, larger pads provide more room for the soldering iron tip.
